entry.title: Oh No, The Phones
entry.summary: Mom’s phone number was 620. If a friend wanted to reach her on her family’s farm just outside the rural Missouri town of Alma (pop. 400, more or less), they had to buzz the operator at the Alma Telephone Company and ask for the Corders or say, “Give me 620, please.” The operator, who probably knew by heart which circuit the Corders were on, would ring line No. 6 with the prescribed sequence: two long rings, zero short rings. The phones in 10 or so households all along the party line would let loose, with the ring pattern signaling to the other farmsteads that the call was for the Corder household. But anyone who wanted to pick it up could—and sometimes did. “You could usually tell when somebody else was on the line,” Mom said. Most often that somebody was Grandma Dieckhoff, who lived one house down the line with her son’s family. The ever-present possibility of eavesdroppers disciplined Mom’s high school chatter—except when it supercharged it: “We sometimes exaggerated a little to give her something to talk about.” Mom remembers precisely when her parents finally got off the party line, much later than most of the U.S.: December 1972, her freshman year at the University of Missouri. Late-adopting Alma Telephone skipped over rotary phones altogether, heading straight to direct dial. Grandma and Grandpa called her up, marveling at the ability simply to punch in 10 numbers to reach her, and only her.

entry.title: Voyager 1, A Day Of Light Away
entry.summary: Humans have trouble with inhuman distances. Miles are about the largest comprehensible unit of measurement we have, because we can understand miles. Watering hole is in a mile? No problem, we’ll be there soon. Aurochs herd is 30 miles away? OK, our hunting party won't walk that in a day, but it’s doable. Miles are a good measure for us, and on the scale of the universe, absolutely useless. The Sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. Can that possibly be spatially encompassed by a human mind that evolved to think in terms of footsteps? The nearest star after that is about 25 trillion miles away . We have the words, but they blur into a meaningless litany of zeroes and -illions. How big is the observable universe? 546,710,000,000,000,000,000,000 miles across, best we can tell. What does that mean to us? Nothing. I submit that while it’s less accurate, it’s more truthful to say simply that the universe is “very big.” Enter light. The fastest thing there is, light travels through a vacuum at 186,000 miles per second, which gives us a helpful benchmark for talking about cosmic distances. (And, in a universe where everything is flying around in different directions, light travels at the same speed from any reference point, which is not intuitive but very helpful. Good job, Einstein.) So 186,000 miles is called a light-second. A light-year, naturally, is the distance it takes light to travel in a year. We can say that Proxima Centauri, alluded to in the previous paragraph, is 25 trillion miles away, or we can say that it’s about four light-years away. Guess which astronomers prefer.

entry.title: Waiting For Jensen
entry.summary: SAN JOSE, Calif. — "Excuse me, can you move so I can take a photo?" a woman asked me and my friend Adam, referring to the large plaque above us bearing seven photos and an inscription: The Booth That Launched A Multi-Trillion-Dollar Company. How could we deny a fellow pilgrim this humble reliquary? We were all here on this rainy Sunday evening to feel the weight of history settle lightly on our shoulders, and also to have some pancakes. We shuffled out into the otherwise empty room while she took a couple pictures, her solemn bearing occasionally quivering out into a quarter of a grin. For Steve Jobs, inspiration struck in the garage at 2066 Crist Drive in Los Altos. For Mark Zuckerberg, there was Room H33 at Harvard's Kirkland House Dorm. For Jensen Huang and his Nvidia co-founders, it all started at the Denny's at 2484 Berryessa Road in San Jose, specifically the big booth in the far corner. Those looking to get closer to the Huang story have few options. You'll have a hard time founding a $4 trillion company, cheating on Jensen Huang's wife, or unwittingly passing on sensitive information to the Chinese government via a mysterious business executive. You have to go back to the beginning. Before Huang was the load-bearing joist propping up the American stock market and an alleged disgrace to the leather jacket community, he was simply a tech worker kicking around Silicon Valley during the first boom. The foundational myth of Nvidia, and by extension Huang, is grounded in the mundane social reality of life in Silicon Valley in some critical ways.

entry.title: ‘Paranormal Activity’ On Broadway Has Some Good Scares, But Not Much Else
entry.summary: It’s hard to overstate just how absurd we thought the whole thing was, even as we purchased tickets and organized getting to the theater. A Paranormal Activity play. Not a musical, I stressed, though my friends and I kept laughing at how funny that idea seemed. I don’t live in New York and am therefore distant from its many stage sensations, though I’ve been hearing about movies and TV shows, well-known IP, popping up on Broadway for years. I remember when the American Psycho musical premiered with Doctor Who (Matt Smith) in the starring role in London in 2013, when they turned The King’s Speech into a play the year before. I was particularly taken with the Once musical as a teenager, though less so with the Moulin Rouge! musical that added more contemporary songs to the jukebox. Last year, Stranger Things: The First Shadow made its way to New York from the UK, a whirlwind of impressive special effects and basically nothing else. Then Instagram ads for Paranormal Activity populated my feed in late August. I thought maybe a nationwide rescreening was being teased for Halloween. It’s been almost 20 years since the first installment came out, so why not? But I’d missed the tag that read “A New Story Live on Broadway” until a close friend whose critical opinion I value said she was going to see it. I’m an evangelist for the third Paranormal Activity movie, but that’s only because I’m an evangelist for the found-footage form, and that film’s admittedly dumb but effective scares are still some of my favorites.

entry.title: Aidan Hutchinson Ended The Patriots’ Season, And Then His Own, On One Play
entry.summary: The Detroit Lions beat the reeling New England Patriots, 35-10, in Munich on Sunday. The new NFC North leaders put up almost 500 total yards on offense, with half-German Amon-Ra St. Brown scoring twice on four catches and Jahmyr Gibbs continuing to make his "best player in football" case with 252 total yards and two touchdowns. It was a great win for the Lions, except for one play that simultaneously took out two stars and might have altered the course of the season for both teams. On New England's first drive of the game, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson got through beleaguered Pats left tackle Will Campbell and took a wide-open angle at quarterback Drake Maye, who couldn't do anything but take a sack and protect the ball. What he couldn't protect, though, was his right ankle, which got caught at an odd angle on the Munich grass. Hutchinson, meanwhile, celebrated his sixth sack of the season, running about 10 yards away and jumping into the air for a fist pump. That's when everything went to shit. Hutchinson landed awkwardly on his right leg and immediately crumpled to the ground in pain. Detroit's team doctors ran out to check on him as he held onto his right knee. He left the game and eventually returned to the locker room.

entry.title: Irreal: EWW As The Default Buffer
entry.summary:
made EWW his default browswer. That means that whenever he clicks on a URL and certain other links, the link is opened in EWW or—for special links—in another application that runs in Emacs. The point is, all browser activity starts in Emacs, usually in EWW.
Of course, Emacs can’t handle every browsing task so Blais uses the & key in EWW to escape to a “normal” browser. Blais says that EWW suffices for 85–90 percent of his use cases. He has some functions to kick off Emacs apps for MP4, PDF, and other specialized links. Everything else goes to EWW. He’s added a couple of custom bindings for EWW functions he uses a lot but it’s mostly a normal EWW instance.
Blais’ experiment shows that it is possible to almost browse from within Emacs. Sites that rely on JavaScript in an essential way are not going to work of course, and there are still a lot sites that insist on JavaScript so they can enforce the delivery of ads or implement a pay wall. Blais’ method gives us a chance to consider if those sites are worth viewing.

journey from Vim to Emacs. Actually, his journey was from Nano to Emacs by way of Vim. When he first started using Linux, Nano was the default editor and he began with that. entry.title: Irreal: Setting The Timezone In Emacs
entry.summary:
hint for those of you who travel and phone home with Emacs. Here’s the situation: you are travelling and log into your home server with SSH and emacsclient. It’s wonderful. Just like being at home except the date/time stamp is wrong. The time and date are whatever your home server thinks they are but you want them to be local time.
The answer is simple. You simply need to change the TZ (timezone) environment variable to reflect your current location. For example, if you’ve travelled to New York (in the US) you would set TZ to “America/New_York”. Emacs, of course, provides a command to do this: (setenv "TZ" "America/New_York").
The zone codes can be a bit opaque so Choi has added a command to the latest Casual suite to set the TZ variable complete with completion. Take a look at his post if you’re interested.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Setting the Timezone in Emacs
entry.summary:
Here’s the problem: You are traveling in a different time zone from the Emacs server instance you are accessing remotely via ssh + emacsclient. All clock calculations in that Emacs session are using the local timezone relative to where the server is located. But what you really want is emacsclient to use the current timezone you are in, so things like the mode line clock render accordingly. To adjust the timezone in an Emacs session, use the command setenv to set the environment variable TZ with a timezone defined in the zoneinfo database. This can be called from Elisp as shown below.
1
(setenv "TZ" "Asia/Seoul")
The latest v3.1.0 update of Casual adds the command casual-timezone-set-tz that provides a completion interface for selecting a timezone to pass to setenv.
1
M-x casual-timezone-set-tz RET
Note that setting TZ impacts the Emacs session globally; any other running behavior depending on a clock should be taken into account.

entry.title: Raymond Zeitler: Creating a Note While org-capture is Active Can Be Confusing
entry.summary:
org-capture and then create a note1 while the capture is active (as I'm doing now), you might be very surprised when you press C-c C-c to finish the note -- it vanishes! Don't Panic! In order to see the note, you'll need to press C-c C-c a second time to complete the capture. Then org-capture adds the item into the Org file, along with the note.
My preference in this situation is to write only the first phrase or sentence of the note. Then I issue the two presses of C-c C-c and complete the note at its destination. I do this not only to avoid the "scary missing note" scenario; I also worry about leaving work unsaved for any amount of time. The computers I grew up with were prone to crashing at inopportune times, so I adopted the motto, "Save Early; save often." An Org note is composed in the *Org Note* buffer, which has no file associated with it and therefore is not a good candidate for saving. 1 With C-c C-z (org-add-note)

entry.title: Irreal: Journelly 1.5
entry.summary:
the release of Journelly 1.5. It’s the formal release of the beta version that I recently wrote about. I can’t say enough about this release. As I’ve said before, my Journelly database is over 4 thousand entries long and before this release Journelly was getting laggy and hard to use but this release resolved all those problems. Now Journelly is as snappy as it was when I had only a few entries and everything about it seems faster and easier.
But wait. There’s more. Ramírez has added an “on this day” feature as well as adding features that make searching for entries by date easier.
If you use Journelly as a journal, you may be interested in the new “on this day” feature. There’s a new button that will show you entries happening on the same day from other years. My particular use case for Journelly is as a memo book so I have no use for this feature. Fortunately, the new Journelly makes it easy to toggle it off if you don’t want it.
The other new significant feature is enhanced searching by date. In the search function you can use on: keyword with several different date formats to search for entries with a particular date. There’s also a calendar button that lets you choose the date from a calendar presentation if you prefer.
You may wonder why I have this entry tagged emacs. I consider Journelly intrinsically linked with Emacs because Journelly keeps its database in an Org file and that means that I can use Emacs and Org mode to search and edit that database. That doesn’t seem like much but I find myself doing it all the time. Journelly has become integrated into my Emacs workflow and become an important part of it.
In the mean time, those of you not in the Journelly beta program now have access to these updates. I can’t speak for Ramírez, of course, but if you’d like to be in the beta program, email Ramírez. He’ll probably be glad to add you.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish
entry.summary: Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.” With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish. Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file: Export the Org file to a specified export backend. View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool. Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends. Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee. Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

entry.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb
entry.summary:
After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player. Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images. So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead. tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but… The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use. Things are now faster:
The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash. I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster… but gives the wrong result most of the time. No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini! So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque. Sort of: I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.
It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.
It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.
Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.
Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.
Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.
Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.
rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.
Emacs asks mpv to display it.
Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.
If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.
(repeat 8-9).
Couldn’t be simpler.
